title: Why we use organic cotton
excerpt: Conventional cotton is one of the most chemically intensive crops on earth. Here's why we made the switch, what it actually means for the fabric, and why we think it matters.
content:
Conventional cotton uses roughly 16% of the world's insecticides and 7% of its pesticides — despite being grown on just 2.4% of the world's farmland. Those numbers are hard to ignore when you're making clothes.
When we started The Break Surf, we knew we wanted to make things properly. That meant thinking about the full picture — not just how a garment performs on the trail, but what went into making it. Organic cotton was the obvious starting point.
GOTS-certified organic cotton is grown without synthetic pesticides or fertilisers, using methods that support soil health and reduce water consumption. The certification also covers the entire supply chain — so we know the mills processing our fabric meet the same standards.
The honest truth is that organic cotton costs more. Our Boulder Tee takes a hit on margin compared to a conventional equivalent. But we'd rather make fewer things at a higher standard than flood the market with cheap kit that ends up in landfill after a season.
The fabric itself is noticeably different too — it has a weight and softness that comes from not being stripped by chemicals during processing. Once you've worn a properly made organic cotton tee, it's hard to go back.
We're not claiming to be perfect. There's still a long way to go in understanding the full impact of everything we make. But using organic cotton is one concrete step we can point to and say: this is better, and we can prove it.

title: Our first community litter pick
excerpt: Last Saturday we took fifteen people, a lot of bags, and a healthy amount of caffeine out to the local nature reserve. Here's what happened.
content:
We've been talking about running a litter pick since the very beginning. It felt like the right thing to do — we make outdoor clothing, the outdoors matters to us, and picking up litter is about as direct an action as it gets.
The first one was smaller than we'd imagined. Fifteen people showed up on a grey October morning, which felt like a win given the weather forecast the night before. We split into three groups and covered about four kilometres of trail and riverbank over two hours.
The haul: 23 bags of general waste, two car tyres, one shopping trolley (always one shopping trolley), and an inexplicable amount of golf balls. The golf balls remain a mystery.
What struck us most was how quickly people got into it. There's something oddly satisfying about leaving a stretch of trail visibly cleaner than you found it. A few people who came along not knowing anyone left swapping numbers to come back next month.
We're planning to make these monthly. The next one is on the first Saturday of November — details will go up on our Instagram. Bring gloves, wear something you don't mind getting muddy, and we'll sort the bags and grabbers.
If you want to get involved or know a spot that could do with some attention, drop us a message. The more people, the more ground we can cover.

title: Designing the Venture Trail Trouser
excerpt: Two years of prototypes, one very patient friend with a sewing machine, and the question we kept coming back to: why do hiking trousers have to look like hiking trousers?
content:
The Venture Trail Trouser started with a frustration. Every technical trouser we could find either performed well and looked terrible, or looked decent and fell apart the moment you took them off tarmac. We couldn't find anything we'd actually want to wear into town after a day out.
The brief we gave ourselves was simple: make a trouser that works on a ridge, works in a gallery, and doesn't announce itself as outdoor clothing from across the room.
The fabric took the longest to get right. We went through eleven samples before landing on the stretch-canvas blend — 72% cotton, 24% nylon, 4% elastane. Cotton gives it the weight and drape that makes it look like proper clothing. The nylon and elastane give it the durability and movement it needs on uneven terrain.
The patterning was the other major puzzle. Articulated knees sound like a small detail but they make an enormous difference to how a trouser moves. We went through six versions of the knee panel before it stopped pulling when you raised your leg.
The relaxed-through-the-seat, tapered-from-the-knee silhouette came from looking at workwear as much as outdoor clothing. Painters' trousers, Japanese field trousers, old military surplus. Things made to move in, that happened to look good.
We're still not done. The next version will have a slightly cleaner waistband and we're looking at a water-resistant finish for the outer layer. But the current version is something we're proud of — a trouser that does what it says without shouting about it.

title: Recycled polyester — what it actually means
excerpt: Recycled polyester is everywhere right now. But what does it actually mean, and is it genuinely better? We looked into it.
content:
Recycled polyester — usually labelled rPET — is polyester made from post-consumer plastic, most commonly PET bottles. The bottles are collected, cleaned, broken down into chips, and spun into fibre. The Summit Fleece uses 280gsm recycled polyester fleece made entirely from rPET.
The environmental case for it is reasonably strong. Producing rPET uses significantly less energy than virgin polyester — estimates vary, but the figure commonly cited is around 30-50% less. It also diverts plastic from landfill or the ocean, which is a direct and measurable benefit.
The more complicated issue is microplastics. Polyester — recycled or otherwise — sheds microfibres when washed, and those fibres end up in waterways. This is an industry-wide problem that doesn't have a clean solution yet. We'd recommend using a Guppyfriend wash bag, which catches a significant proportion of shed fibres.
We're honest about the fact that rPET isn't a silver bullet. The ideal is to move away from synthetic fibres altogether for most garments. But for a mid-layer fleece, there's currently no natural-fibre alternative that performs the same way at the same weight. In that context, rPET is the better choice.
The certification matters too. Our supplier is bluesign-certified, which covers energy use, water consumption, and chemical management across the manufacturing process. It's not a perfect system, but it's a meaningful independent check.
We'll keep reviewing this as the industry develops. If a better option becomes available at a price point that works, we'll switch. Until then, rPET is where we are.
